sections.title: Vitamins and physiological function
sections.text:
Vitamins are needed in small amounts but support essential processes. Their function often depends on enzymes, transport and interactions with other nutrients. A deficiency sign is not always specific to one vitamin, and excess intake can also cause harm. Classification by solubility helps explain absorption and storage but does not divide vitamins into “always safe” and “always toxic”.

**vitamins.**

Vitamins are organic nutrients needed in small amounts for normal biological function. Many act as coenzymes or contribute to signaling, immunity, blood formation and tissue maintenance. They do not provide dietary energy in the same way as carbohydrate, protein or fat.

**Fat-soluble versus water-soluble vitamins.**

| Fat-soluble | Water-soluble |
|---|---|
| Vitamins A, D, E and K | Vitamin C and the B-complex |
| Absorption is closely associated with fat digestion | Absorbed through different water-compatible transport pathways |
| Some can be stored substantially in tissues | Many have more limited reserves |
| Excess intake of certain vitamins can cause toxicity | Excess intake can also cause harm, depending on the vitamin |

**Classification: ADEK = fat-soluble vitamins.**

**Complete vitamin comparison.**

| Vitamin | Principal functions | Important dietary sources | Classic deficiency association |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (retinoids) | Vision, epithelial integrity, immunity | Eggs, dairy, liver, provitamin A carotenoid-rich vegetables | Night blindness, xerophthalmia |
| B1 (thiamine) | Carbohydrate metabolism, nerve function | Whole grains, pulses, meat | Beriberi |
| B2 (riboflavin) | FAD/FMN-dependent energy metabolism | Milk, eggs, meats, some greens | Cheilosis, glossitis |
| B3 (niacin) | NAD/NADP coenzymes | Meat, fish, grains, legumes | Pellagra |
| B5 (pantothenic acid) | Coenzyme A formation | Widely distributed in foods | Deficiency rare |
| B6 (pyridoxine family) | Amino-acid metabolism, neurotransmitter synthesis | Meat, fish, legumes, grains | Anemia, neurological symptoms |
| B7 (biotin) | Carboxylase reactions | Eggs, nuts and varied foods | Dermatitis, neurological manifestations |
| B9 (folate) | DNA synthesis, one-carbon metabolism | Leafy vegetables, pulses, fortified foods | Megaloblastic anemia; neural-tube-defect risk |
| B12 (cobalamin) | DNA synthesis, nervous-system function | Animal-source foods, fortified foods | Megaloblastic anemia and neurological damage |
| C (ascorbic acid) | Collagen synthesis, antioxidant functions | Citrus, guava, peppers | Scurvy |
| D | Calcium–phosphorus regulation, skeletal mineralization | Fortified foods, fish; also skin synthesis with UV exposure | Rickets, osteomalacia |
| E | Antioxidant defense | Nuts, seeds, plant oils | Neuromuscular complications in severe deficiency |
| K | Activation of clotting-related proteins | Leafy vegetables and other foods | Bleeding tendency |

Deficiencies are biological syndromes, not one-to-one diagnostic tests. More than one nutrient deficiency or disease may produce similar symptoms.

**Why does vitamin A deficiency cause night blindness.**

Rhodopsin is a light-sensitive pigment in retinal rod photoreceptors. Its visual cycle involves retinal, a vitamin A-derived molecule. Insufficient vitamin A can disrupt dark adaptation, making vision under dim illumination difficult. Prolonged serious deficiency can also damage eye tissues.

**Why does vitamin C deficiency cause scurvy.**

Vitamin C contributes to the hydroxylation reactions needed for normal collagen synthesis. Collagen is an important structural protein in connective tissues. Severe vitamin C deficiency can impair connective-tissue integrity, contributing to bleeding gums, poor wound healing and other manifestations.

**Why is vitamin D important for bones.**

Vitamin D helps regulate intestinal absorption and body handling of calcium and phosphorus. Inadequate vitamin D can impair bone mineralization. In children, severe deficiency can cause rickets. In adults, impaired mineralization may cause osteomalacia.

Vitamin B12 illustrates an important exception to the general tendency for water-soluble vitamins to have limited reserves: substantial body stores can delay deficiency. Folate and B12 deficiencies can both cause megaloblastic blood changes, but B12 deficiency can also damage nervous tissue. Improving a blood picture does not necessarily correct the neurological problem. Nutritional assessment therefore requires more than matching one symptom with one nutrient.

sections.title: Minerals, absorption and bioavailability
sections.text:
**minerals.**

Dietary minerals are inorganic elements required for physiological processes. Some are needed in comparatively large amounts, while others are required only in trace quantities.

**Major minerals.**

| Mineral | Main function | Sources | Deficiency-related concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calcium | Bones, teeth, muscle and nerve function | Dairy, fortified foods, selected greens | Impaired bone health |
| Phosphorus | ATP, bones, nucleic acids | Dairy, meat, legumes | Deficiency uncommon but consequential |
| Magnesium | Enzyme functions and neuromuscular activity | Nuts, legumes, whole grains | Neuromuscular/metabolic disturbances |
| Potassium | Membrane electrical function and fluid regulation | Fruit, vegetables, pulses | Weakness, arrhythmias in severe deficiency |
| Sodium | Extracellular fluid and electrical signaling | Salt, many foods | Low levels can disturb neurological function |
| Chloride | Fluid balance and gastric acid | Table salt and foods | Electrolyte disturbances |

**Trace minerals.**

| Mineral | Important role | Deficiency association |
|---|---|---|
| Iron | Hemoglobin and oxygen transport | Iron-deficiency anemia |
| Iodine | Thyroid hormone synthesis | Goitre, developmental impairment |
| Zinc | Enzymes, immunity, growth and wound healing | Poor growth or impaired immunity |
| Selenium | Antioxidant and thyroid-related selenoproteins | Specific deficiency syndromes |
| Copper | Enzyme systems and iron metabolism | Hematological and neurological abnormalities |
| Fluoride | Influences tooth-enamel resistance | Low exposure may increase dental-caries susceptibility; excess causes fluorosis |

**Why is iron important.**

Hemoglobin in red blood cells contains iron-bearing heme groups. These reversibly bind oxygen, supporting oxygen transport from lungs to tissues. Insufficient iron can impair hemoglobin production. However, **not all anemia results from iron deficiency**. Folate or B12 deficiency, inherited disorders, inflammation and other causes must also be considered.

**Why is iodine important.**

Iodine is required to synthesize thyroid hormones, principally T₃ and T₄. Thyroid hormones contribute to metabolism, growth and development. Inadequate iodine can produce goitre and, during fetal or early-childhood development, serious neurological consequences. Iodized salt is an important population-level prevention strategy.

Bioavailability is the fraction of an ingested substance available for absorption and physiological use. It depends on chemical form, the food matrix, digestive function and other dietary components. Vitamin C can improve non-haem iron absorption from plant foods through reduction and solubility-related effects, while some food compounds can inhibit it. Total laboratory nutrient content and the amount the body actually uses are different quantities.

Sodium and potassium support electrical gradients and fluid regulation, but their balance depends on kidneys and hormones as well as intake. Calcium supports bone, signalling and contraction, while vitamin D affects its handling. Minerals are required in appropriate amounts; the word “essential” does not imply that unlimited supplementation is beneficial.

sections.title: Dietary reference values and balanced eating
sections.text:
**a balanced diet.**

A balanced diet provides adequate energy and essential nutrients while supporting health and avoiding harmful excesses. WHO identifies four central principles:

**Adequacy:** Provides necessary nutrients.

**Balance:** Appropriate energy and nutrient proportions.

**Moderation:** Limits components that may increase health risks.

**Diversity:** Includes different nutrient-dense foods.

A balanced diet is not defined by one universal meal or a requirement to eat equal quantities of every food group.

**an RDA.**

RDA stands for **Recommended Dietary Allowance**. It represents a dietary intake level estimated to meet the needs of nearly all healthy people in a specified age–sex or physiological group, under the relevant nutrient reference framework. Other reference measures include:

**EAR:** Estimated Average Requirement.

**AI:** Adequate Intake.

**UL:** Tolerable Upper Intake Level.

These values are not interchangeable.

**Malnutrition: Not simply starvation.**

Malnutrition includes undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies or excesses, and overweight or obesity.

| Type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Undernutrition | Inadequate energy or nutrient availability |
| Stunting | Low length/height for age in children |
| Wasting | Low weight for height/length, or equivalent assessment criteria |
| Underweight | Low weight for age |
| Micronutrient deficiency | Inadequate vitamin or mineral status |
| Overnutrition | Excessive energy or selected nutrient exposure |
| Obesity | Excess adiposity affecting health |

A person can have excess body weight while simultaneously experiencing micronutrient deficiencies. This is one form of the **double burden of malnutrition**.

A balanced pattern combines nutrient adequacy, suitable energy intake, variety and moderation. Whole grains, pulses, vegetables, fruit and appropriate protein sources can contribute different nutrients. Requirements vary with age, body size, activity, pregnancy, lactation and health. General reference values for populations are not individualized treatment prescriptions. [WHO: healthy diet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/healthy-diet).

Energy balance is dynamic: intake, expenditure and body stores interact over time. Body mass index is mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, but it does not directly measure body fat or distinguish every person's body composition. Anthropometric measures are screening tools interpreted alongside age, growth patterns and clinical context.

sections.title: Digestion, metabolism and the double burden
sections.text:
Digestion and absorption are developed in Chapter 12; cellular energy pathways in Chapter 10. Nutrition connects these processes with actual food availability and physiological need. Adequate food intake may still fail to produce adequate nutrition if infection, malabsorption or unsuitable dietary composition impairs nutrient use.

Undernutrition, micronutrient deficiency and excess adiposity can coexist within a country, household or individual. Child growth indicators describe different dimensions: stunting concerns height for age, wasting weight relative to height, and underweight weight for age. They should not be treated as interchangeable diagnoses. Food security, sanitation, maternal health and health services all influence nutritional outcomes.

questions.prompt: A laboratory receives an unknown food sample and needs to test whether its nutrients can be absorbed and used. Which concept is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Bioavailability concerns the fraction of a substance that becomes available for relevant absorption and physiological use.

questions.prompt: A severe deficiency of vitamin C impairs collagen formation. Which biochemical role is directly relevant?

options.A: Formation of bile salts from sodium
options.C: Support for hydroxylation reactions in collagen biosynthesis

questions.explanation: Vitamin C supports enzymes involved in collagen hydroxylation, so deficiency affects connective-tissue integrity.

questions.prompt: A person with severe thiamine deficiency is at risk of:

options.C: Scurvy due exclusively to low calcium

questions.explanation: Vitamin B1 is needed for important energy-metabolism reactions and nerve function; severe deficiency causes beriberi.

questions.prompt: Why can treating a folate-deficiency-like blood picture without checking vitamin B12 status be problematic?

options.B: Vitamin B12 has no neurological function
options.C: All anemia is caused by iron
options.D: B12 deficiency may involve neurological injury even when certain blood changes improve

questions.explanation: Folate can affect hematologic manifestations while B12-associated neurological injury requires its own diagnosis and treatment.

questions.prompt: Which dietary mineral is structurally required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones?
questions.explanation: Iodine is incorporated into thyroid hormones T3 and T4, which contribute to metabolism and development.

questions.prompt: Which food component commonly improves absorption of non-heme iron from plant foods when consumed together?
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid can improve non-heme iron absorption partly through chemical reduction and solubility-related effects.
